content.paragraph: Before starting this section, you might need to review the trigonometric functions. In particular, it is important to remember that when we talk about the function $$f$$ defined for all real numbers $$x$$ by

it is understood that $$\sin x$$ means the sine of the angle whose radian measure is $$x$$ . A similar convention holds for the other trigonometric functions $$\cos$$ , $$\tan$$ , $$\csc$$ , $$\sec$$ , and $$\cot$$ . Recall from Section 2.5 that all of the trigonometric functions are continuous at every number in their domains.

subsection.title: Derivatives of the Trigonometric Functions
subsection.paragraph: If we sketch the graph of the function $$f(x) = \sin x$$ and use the interpretation of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ as the slope of the tangent to the sine curve in order to sketch the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ (see Exercise 2.8.16), then it looks as if the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ may be the same as the cosine curve (see Figure 1).

figure.alt_text: Two graphs display a curve on the x y coordinate plane one below the other such that their tick marks are aligned. The origin of the first and the second graphs are vertically aligned. In both the graphs, the x axis is displayed from negative 2 pi to 2 pi in increments of pi/2 units. In both the graphs, the curve increases and decreases with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each maximum and minimum. The curve labeled y = f(x) = sin(x) enters the third quadrant, goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at (negative 2 pi, 0), reaches a high point at (negative 3 pi/2, 1), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), falls below the x axis, reaches a low point at (negative pi/2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right through the origin until it reaches a high point at (pi/2, 1). It then goes down and to the right through (pi, 0), reaches a minimum at (3 pi/2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right through (2 pi, 0), and continues in this fashion as it proceeds to the right. The horizontal tangents which are lying above the curve touch the sine curve exactly once at its high points. The horizontal tangents which are lying below the curve touch the sine curve exactly once at its low points. The tangents with a negative slope almost appear to lie along the sine curve and touch it exactly once at (negative pi, 0) and (pi, 0). A tangent with a positive slope almost appears to lie along the curve while rising through the origin and touches it exactly once at the origin. In the second graph, the curve y = f prime (x) enters the second quadrant, rises to a high point (negative 2 pi, 1), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative 3 pi/2, 0), goes down and to the right, reaches a low point at (negative pi, negative 1), goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis again at (negative pi/2, 0), and reaches a high point at (0, 1). It then goes down and to the right by crossing the x axis at (pi/2, 0), reaches a low point at (pi, negative 1), again goes up and to the right, crossing the x axis at (3 pi/2, 0), then reaches a high point again at (2 pi, 1), and continues in this fashion as it proceeds to the right. The high and low points of the sine curve are vertically aligned with the x-intercepts of y = f prime (x). Similarly, the x-intercepts of the sine curve are vertically aligned with the high and low points of y = f prime (x).

subsection.paragraph: Trigonometric functions are often used in modeling real-world phenomena. In particular, vibrations, waves, elastic motions, and other quantities that vary in a periodic manner can be described using trigonometric functions. In the following example we discuss an instance of simple harmonic motion.

problem.paragraph: Solution The velocity and acceleration are

The object oscillates from the lowest point $$\left( {s = 4{cm}} \right)$$ to the highest point $$\left( {s = - 4{cm}} \right)$$ . The period of the oscillation is $$2\pi$$ , the period of $$\cos t$$ .

The speed is $$|\upsilon| = 4\left| {\sin t} \right|$$ , which is greatest when $$\left| {\sin t} \right| = 1$$ , that is, when $$\cos t = 0$$ . So the object moves fastest as it passes through its equilibrium position $$\left( {s = 0} \right)$$ . Its speed is $$0$$ when $$\sin t = 0$$ , that is, at the highest and lowest points.
The acceleration $$a = - 4\cos t = 0$$ when $$s = 0$$ . It has greatest magnitude at the highest and lowest points. See the graphs in Figure 5.
